subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
passage: I'm Lalit. Three years ago, after a good bonus, I paid for a computer lab in a school in a district I'd read about. Twenty machines, new desks, a ribbon-cutting. I was proud. I had never asked the school what it needed. Power there went off for most of the day with no backup, and no one on the staff had been taught to use the machines. When I visited a year later, Pradeep, the headmaster, walked me into the room. The screens were under plastic sheets and the door was kept locked to protect them. He said the teachers would have preferred a roof that didn't leak. That stayed with me. I had made a gift that fitted my picture of help, not their school.

qa.q: How many machines were in the lab?
qa.a: There were twenty machines in the lab.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling at the ribbon-cutting, and how did it change at the later visit?
qa.a: Lalit felt proud at the ribbon-cutting, but at the later visit felt regretful and humbled on seeing the covered screens and locked door.

qa.q: What could Lalit have done differently before paying for the lab?
qa.a: Lalit could have asked the school what it needed and started small with backup power and teacher training, since a fit with the local situation decides whether equipment gets used.

qa.q: How might Pradeep have felt about the lab?
qa.a: Pradeep was probably grateful but frustrated, keeping the room locked to protect it and mentioning that teachers wanted a roof that didn't leak.

grounding: Shows a person funding a school computer lab without power backup or trained teachers, so the equipment sits unused.

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
passage:
School log, Thursday.
Mr Shankar came today to see the lab he gave us last June. Twelve computers, new tables, a banner with his company's name. The room has been locked since Diwali. Power comes for about four hours a day here, mostly after school, and there is no inverter. None of our teachers has used these machines before, so nobody felt confident to take a class in there.
I unlocked it for him. Dust covers on every screen. A few Class 6 children pressed their faces to the window glass as we stood inside.
He was quiet for a long time, then asked why nobody had told him. I said we did not want to seem ungrateful.
Next step: I have asked him to meet our four teachers on Saturday and hear what they actually need before anything else is bought.
— Parveen, Head Teacher

qa.q: How long has the lab been locked?
qa.a: The room has been locked since Diwali.

qa.q: What might Shankar have been feeling when he stood quietly in the dusty lab?
qa.a: He was likely shocked and disappointed, seeing that his gift had been unused for months while children could only look in through the window.

qa.q: What approach could Shankar have tried before buying the computers?
qa.a: He could have asked the teachers first about power and training, and planned a backup supply and teacher sessions along with the machines.

qa.q: How do the Class 6 children at the window experience the unused lab?
qa.a: For them the lab is something to look at but never use, which may feel like a promise that was not kept.

grounding: It shows a donor's computer lab sitting unused in a school with no power backup or trained teachers, so a well-meant gift brings little benefit.

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
passage:
Tuesday night
Went back to Bhimpur school today, first time since we opened the lab in March. I was carrying the photo from the opening ceremony on my phone. All ten tablets charging, children smiling.
Avni Ma'am, the maths teacher, walked me to the room. Locked. Inside, the tablets were stacked in their box. "Power goes by eleven most days," she said. "And nobody showed us how to use the lesson app. The children kept asking. After a while they stopped."
I kept saying, "But we raised the money in three weeks!" as if that fixed anything.
On the bus back I did the maths. The fundraising, the travel, the ceremony, and maybe six hours of use in total.
I planned this from my flat in the city. I never once asked Avni Ma'am what the school needed. Tomorrow I'm going to call her and ask.
— Varun

qa.q: What does Avni Ma'am say happens to the power most days?
qa.a: She says the power goes by eleven most days.

qa.q: How can you tell Varun felt ashamed on the bus back?
qa.a: Varun works out that all the effort bought maybe six hours of use and admits never once asking Avni Ma'am what the school needed.

qa.q: What else could Varun have done first, and why would it help?
qa.a: Varun could have visited and asked the teachers about power and training before raising money, so the plan fit what the school could actually use.

qa.q: How might Avni Ma'am feel about the unused tablets?
qa.a: She may feel frustrated and a little embarrassed, since the children kept asking and the teachers were never shown how to use the lesson app.

grounding: It shows a young organiser discovering that tablets sent to a village school sit unused because there is no power backup and no teacher training.
